name: Spray-tan booth
lead: A spray-tan booth is an enclosed, automated cabin in which a fine mist of a sunless tanning solution is sprayed over the body. The active ingredient is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a colourless sugar that reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a temporary brown colour. Professionals can also apply the solution by hand with an airbrush. [1]

The colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as the outer skin sheds, and it does not involve ultraviolet exposure, which is why sunless tanning is often presented as an alternative to sunbeds. [1] The US Food and Drug Administration has approved DHA for external use but not for use around the eyes or lips, on mucous membranes, or by inhalation, and Wikipedia notes that all-over booth spraying can make that exposure hard to avoid. [1]
Laboratory and animal studies have reported cell damage and lung effects after DHA exposure. No human trials of booth-related inhalation outcomes were found. [2][3][4]

paras: DHA is not a dye or paint. It reacts with amino acids in the skin's dead outer layer in a Maillard-type reaction, and erythrulose, sometimes combined with it, works similarly but develops more slowly. The colour lasts as long as the treated cells remain in the outer layer. [1] Booths deliver the solution as a mist in a shower-like enclosure, whereas other formats include hand airbrushing and home sprays and aerosols. [1]

Eva Wittgenstein at Cincinnati Children's Hospital observed in the 1950s that DHA stained skin brown. Man-Tan, the first commercial DHA self-tanner, appeared in 1959, followed by Coppertone's QT in 1960, and both produced orange-toned results that harmed the category's reputation. Reformulations and, from the late 1990s, automated spray booths broadened the market. [1]

According to the FDA position summarised by Wikipedia, inhalation and mucous-membrane exposure are the concern with booth application. The same article reports a toxicologist's concern that DHA deposited in the lungs could be absorbed into the bloodstream, a 2004 cell study finding DNA damage and apoptosis, and a 2007 study finding more free radicals in DHA-treated skin under sun exposure. It also reports a 2010 European Commission scientific committee opinion that DHA spray tanning posed no risk, which specialists criticised because industry supplied much of the evidence. [1]

Contact dermatitis from DHA or erythrulose has been reported, and some products contain fragrances or parabens. [1] Sunscreen in some tanning products may not give lasting protection, because avobenzone can degrade in UVA light. [1] A UK Health and Safety Executive study explored occupational health risks for beauty therapists who carry out spray tanning. [5]

No studies found that tested spray-tan booths in human volunteers for health or appearance outcomes. Related laboratory and animal work includes cell studies in which DHA suppressed nutrient signalling and induced mitochondrial stress in liver cells, caused genotoxicity and chromosomal instability in lung, heart and liver cell models, and induced cell-cycle arrest and cell death in a melanoma cell line. [6][2][7][8] A 2025 mouse study reported lung inflammation and fibrosis after inhaled DHA. [3] These findings apply to cells and animals at the exposures tested, and their relevance to booth use has not been established in humans.

Survey research describes who uses sunless tanning. An analysis of US National Health Interview Survey data looked at spray tanning, self-applied lotion tanning and indoor UV tanning among non-Hispanic white women aged 18 to 49. [9] A cross-sectional study estimated indoor tanning prevalence among US adults. [10] An analysis of the 2016 ban on commercial solaria in Australia used search trends to assess consumer interest in indoor and spray tanning. [11] A New Zealand audit counted businesses offering sunbeds and spray tanning. [12]

Spray tanning is promoted as a way to get a tan without UV exposure, which dermatology and public health sources link to melanoma risk. A study of undergraduates on the US Gulf Coast examined intentional tanning behaviours in a population with elevated melanoma mortality. [13] Community discussion about booths was not available for this entry.

card.summary: Automated booth that mists DHA for a UV-free tan; the colour is reliable, but inhalation safety is unstudied in humans.
card.note: FDA approves DHA for external use only, not inhalation; cell and mouse studies report harm at tested doses.

quick.overview:
A spray-tan booth coats the body in a mist of dihydroxyacetone (DHA), which turns the outer skin layer brown without UV light. The colour fades over about 5 to 10 days.

The tanning effect itself is well described. What has not been tested in people is the effect of breathing the mist.
quick.mechanism: DHA reacts with amino acids in dead surface skin cells in a Maillard-type browning reaction. The colour fades as those cells shed.
quick.risks: The FDA has approved DHA for external use only, not for the eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation, and booth spraying can make that exposure difficult to avoid. Cell and mouse studies report DNA damage, cell stress and lung inflammation; no human trials of booth inhalation were found. Contact dermatitis has been reported.
